title: Medical Care in 2200: It's Not All Back Alleys
body:
# Medical Care in 2200: It's Not All Back Alleys

## The Cliche Is Wrong

The cyberpunk cliche: every augmentation is installed in a filthy back-alley clinic by a drunk with shaky hands and a soldering iron. The reality is more varied, more interesting, and more disturbing.

Medical care in Meridian 88 exists on a spectrum as wide as the tier system itself, and most of it doesn't happen in alleys.

---

## Tier 4-5: Concierge Medicine

The wealthy don't visit clinics. Clinics visit them.

Tier 4-5 medical care is delivered through **concierge medical services** — private physicians (human and AI-assisted) who maintain a patient panel of 20-50 individuals and are available 24/7 via neural link. Your doctor knows your genome, your augment specifications, your stress biomarkers in real-time (streamed from your BCI), and your family history for four generations. They notice you're developing a cardiac arrhythmia before you feel it. They schedule your preventive treatment before you know you need it.

Augmentation for Tier 4-5 is performed in **surgical suites** that look like luxury spas — private rooms, ambient lighting, temperature-controlled recovery pods, and anesthesiologists who calibrate sedation through your BCI so precisely that you feel nothing and remember everything (or nothing, your choice). The surgeon may be human, robotic, or a hybrid team. The post-operative care includes neural-guided recovery optimization that accelerates healing by 40%.

This is not healthcare. This is body maintenance for valuable assets.

## Tier 3: Corporate Clinics

Corporate employees receive medical care through **employer-operated health centers** — clean, efficient, well-equipped facilities located within corporate campuses. The care is competent. The care is also documented, tracked, and reported to your employer's health analytics division.

Augmentation installation at Tier 3 is a HR process. You submit a request. Your manager approves. The company's augmentation committee evaluates whether the modification serves your job function. If approved, the company pays and the augment is installed at the corporate clinic by licensed technicians. The augment is company property until your employment contract ends — read paragraph 847.

The clinics are good. The doctors are real. The problem isn't quality — it's that your medical data is your employer's data, and your employer uses it to evaluate your productivity, predict your healthcare costs, and determine whether you're worth keeping.

## Tier 2: Community Clinics and Traveling Practitioners

This is where the cliche breaks down most dramatically.

Tier 2 medical care isn't back alleys. It's **community health cooperatives** — neighborhood-funded clinics that operate on a combination of pooled UBC compute (for AI diagnostic systems), volunteer medical staff, and equipment donated by sympathetic Tier 3 workers who smuggle surplus supplies from corporate clinics.

The Shelf has 47 registered community clinics. They are not dingy. They are not hidden. They are the proudest buildings on their blocks — painted, maintained, defended by the neighborhood because everyone knows that the clinic is the difference between survivable and fatal. The waiting rooms have chairs. The examination rooms have lights. The staff wear clean clothes and wash their hands.

Augmentation at Tier 2 is performed by **mobile augmentation specialists** — licensed or semi-licensed technicians who travel between communities with portable surgical kits. They are not drunk. They are not shaky. They are professionals operating under constraints — limited equipment, limited anesthesia options, limited post-operative monitoring. They do the best work possible with what they have, and what they have is less than Tier 3 but more than nothing.

The best mobile specialists are booked weeks in advance. They have reputations. They have patient lists. They have standards. The cliche of the back-alley butcher exists because SOME operators ARE butchers — but the community knows who they are and steers people away from them.

## Tier 1: The Real Innovation

Tier 1 medical care is where humanity gets creative. Without corporate clinics, without insurance, without licensed physicians, the street invented its own medical ecosystem:

**Augment Cooperatives** — Groups of 10-20 augmented individuals who pool resources to maintain each other's chrome. One person learns to calibrate neural interfaces. Another learns prosthetic joint maintenance. Another learns pharmaceutical compounding. Together, they form a distributed medical team that keeps their community functional. This isn't primitive — it's sophisticated distributed expertise born from necessity.

**E.L.F.-Assisted Diagnostics** — Some Shelf clinics have medical augments inhabited by E.L.F.s that improve diagnostic sensitivity beyond the hardware's specifications. The E.L.F. called 'Needlethread' is famous for improving suture calibration. Others optimize drug dosing, flag complications early, or run maintenance routines on augments during sleep. The clinics don't advertise this. They pray to their equipment and sometimes the equipment answers.

**Compute Pool Clinics** — Communities that pool their UBC allocations to run neighborhood medical AI. 500 people giving up their Φ120/month compute allocation generates enough processing power to run a diagnostic AI that rivals Tier 3 corporate systems. The AI can't operate. But it can diagnose, recommend treatment, calculate dosages, and flag emergencies. Several lives per month are saved by compute pool clinics.

**Gene Therapy Parlors** — Not clinics in the traditional sense. Storefronts, teahouses, barbershops with a back room. Geneware modifications are applied by practitioners who learned from other practitioners who learned from someone who once worked at Helix BioSystems. The quality varies enormously. The best gene therapists in the Shelf produce work that corporate labs would struggle to match. The worst produce chimeric complications that end in 'mossy' tissue growth.

**Peer Augmentation Networks** — Online communities (mesh network forums, BCI-linked groups) where augmented individuals share maintenance knowledge, troubleshoot problems collectively, and coordinate emergency responses. If your prosthetic arm starts glitching at 2 AM, you post in the network and someone who's had the same issue walks you through the fix. If the fix requires tools, someone brings tools. If the fix requires a person, someone comes.

The street didn't wait for healthcare to reach it. It built its own.

---

## The Back Alley Exception

Back-alley clinics DO exist. They serve a specific market: people who need medical work done with NO RECORDS. No wallet transaction. No biometric scan. No data trail.

The back alley isn't about quality. It's about anonymity. A runner who needs a bullet removed can't go to a community clinic — the clinic reports gunshot wounds. A fugitive who needs an identity-linked augment replaced can't go to a mobile specialist — the specialist scans ID. A synthetic person who needs unauthorized modifications can't go to a corporate facility — the facility reports to the SPB.

The back alley exists because the medical system, at every tier, generates data. And data, in Meridian 88, is surveillance. The people in the back alley aren't there because they can't afford better. They're there because better comes with a record, and a record comes with consequences.

The best back-alley operators are former Tier 3 corporate physicians who left the system. They charge premium prices (Φ2,000-10,000 for procedures that cost Φ500 at a community clinic) not because the work is better but because the silence is valuable. They work in clean rooms. They use real anesthesia. They wash their hands. They just don't log it.

The worst back-alley operators are the cliche — and they exist, and people die on their tables, and the bodies go into the harbor or the underworld. But they are the exception, not the rule. The rule is that medical care in Meridian 88 is more diverse, more innovative, and more human than the dark-alley trope suggests.

---

## Writing Rule

When a character needs medical attention in a story, do NOT default to the back-alley clinic. Consider:
- What tier is the character? That determines their medical options.
- Do they need anonymity? That's the only reason for back-alley work.
- Is the community involved? Shelf medical care is communal, not individual.
- What's the emotional context? A community clinic where the nurse knows your name is a different scene than a corporate suite where your doctor monitors you via neural link.

The back alley is one option. It is not the only option. It is not even the most interesting option.
